# STARC Institute (星弧)

> STARC Institute (Chinese name 星弧) is a small nonprofit that helps university students build real products and do real research, as an alternative to the paid "background-boosting" (背景提升) and research-internship industry. No tuition is charged. Admitted students pay a refundable deposit (CNY 1,000 / USD 150) that is returned in full after they complete the program, regardless of whether their project succeeds.

Key facts:
- Main program: the One-Person Company (OPC, 一人公司计划) cohort. 12 students, 8 weeks, about 10 hours a week. Each student builds and launches a real product with AI tools, finds real users, and keeps a weekly build log. Cohort 1 is for undergraduate and master's students at universities in mainland China. Apply through the application form: https://forms.gle/9kHxzd7byt3BKD2k9
- Graduation is judged by evidence (a live product, real usage data, eight build logs), not by a certificate. Two outcomes: Shipped (at least 10 real external users) and Completed (full participation, fewer users). Both get the deposit back.
- The deposit is kept only if a student misses two weekly logs in a row without notice, quits after week 1, or fakes data/work.
- Selective research track (科研合作): rare openings with an active researcher; same refundable deposit; publication is never promised.
- STARC does not ghost-write, does not guarantee outcomes, does not sell follow-up courses or recommendation letters, and never charges before admission.
- Forfeited deposits pay only for operating costs (domain, hosting, tools); a ledger is published after each cohort.
- Students own 100% of what they build; STARC takes no equity, revenue share or credit.
- The team is small and unpaid; names are not listed yet.
- STARC previously charged a USD 300 operating fee for research matching; that fee has been dropped.

## Blog: questions answered
- [Can I build a real product with AI if I can't code?](https://starc.institute/blog/build-product-with-ai-without-coding.html): Yes. AI coding assistants now let a non-programmer build and launch a small, working web product, as long as the problem is narrow and you're willing to read error messages and test everything yourself. The hard part was never typing code. It's choosing a real problem, finding users, and judging whether what the AI produced actually works.
- [Are paid research internships worth it?](https://starc.institute/blog/are-paid-research-internships-worth-it.html): Sometimes, but far less often than the price suggests. A paid program is worth considering only if you'll do real work on a real question with an active researcher, and they'll tell you plainly what you will and won't get. If a program promises a publication, an admission advantage or a recommendation letter in exchange for a fee, treat that as a warning sign, not a feature.
